#9798. New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation

NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes:

All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms.

Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos

🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations.

🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds.

🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together.

🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short.

Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.

Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts.

Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto

Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume.

Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action

Depth: relative distance from the camera.

Segmentation: regions and object boundaries.

Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer

Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks.

Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation.

The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion.

Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized.

Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions.

Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual

Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history.

Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history

Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction.

The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often.

Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips.

Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out.

Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps.

Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal.

Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation.

The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state.

Transfer-auto: Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data.

Sim-auto: Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation.

Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume.

Sim-Bimanual: Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export.

Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence.

#9795. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9793. Debugging macOS LaunchAgent Failures With launchctl and Exit Code 78

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Every morning at 7:45, a job on my Mac runs a reconciliation and posts the results for the finance team. It's an ordinary LaunchAgent: a plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents, a Python script, and a log file.

For three mornings in October, it didn't run.

Nothing told me. There was no error in Slack, because the code that sends errors never started. There was no crash report. And the log file, the first place anyone looks, had nothing new in it, because the job failed before it could write a line.

launchd keeps a record of every job's last exit. Ask for it:

The labels in this post are examples. For a quick look at every job, launchctl list shows the last exit status in its second column.

78 is EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h, a configuration error. My script never exits with 78, and that's the tell: when the exit code is one your program doesn't use, your program probably never ran.

Before launchd starts your program, it does some setup. It opens the files named in StandardOutPath and StandardErrorPath, changes into WorkingDirectory, and finds the executable. If any of that fails, your program never starts, and the job ends with 78.

I wanted to know exactly which mistakes produce it, so I loaded a set of deliberately broken test jobs on macOS 26.6 and read what launchd reported:

Two things surprised me. launchd happily creates a missing log folder, so that's not your problem. And a log file it can't open is fatal. Not a warning and not a quiet fallback: the whole job stops, and the error has nowhere to go.

The worst part of debugging a 7:45 job is the 23-hour feedback loop. You don't need it. Copy the plist, give it a new label, swap the program for something harmless, and tell it to run at load. Everything launchd sets up stays the same, so if the setup is broken, you'll see 78 in two seconds:

/usr/bin/true does nothing and exits 0. If the copy still reports 78, the problem is in the setup, not your code. Fix the plist, rerun the copy, and only then touch the real job. Reload the real one with launchctl bootout and launchctl bootstrap so launchd reads the new version.

Once I'd found one of these, I wanted to check the rest. This script reads every plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents, flags the setups that end in 78, and prints each job's last exit code:

crm-sync is the classic upgrade casualty: Python moved, and the plist still points at the old interpreter. weekly-export is a renamed folder. Both fail silently in exactly the same way mine did, and cash-recon gets flagged before it ever has the chance.

The fix took five minutes. Noticing took three days, because every alert I had lived inside the job, and the job never ran. A job that doesn't start can't report its own failure.

What would have caught it on the first morning is a check that doesn't depend on the job at all: something separate that looks for the job's last success and complains when it's missing. It's the same principle I wrote about in small pipelines fail quietly: watch for the last success, not the last error.

The short version, for every LaunchAgent you rely on:

Your GitHub Actions Cron Job Can Disappear Without Failing

#9789. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9788. Building Data Observability for Banking Pipelines

Data Engineer specialising in Azure, AWS, Databricks, dbt, and scalable data platforms. Writing about Data Engineering, AI, and cloud architecture.

Data Engineer specialising in Azure, AWS, Databricks, dbt, and scalable data platforms. Writing about Data Engineering, AI, and cloud architecture.

Data Engineer specialising in Azure, AWS, Databricks, dbt, and scalable data platforms. Writing about Data Engineering, AI, and cloud architecture.

Loud failures are easy. A job crashes, the scheduler turns red, somebody gets paged, and within the hour there is a chat thread with far too many people in it. Annoying, sure, but the system is at least telling you the truth.

The failure I worry about is the quiet one. Every task shows green. The report lands on time. And one number inside it is wrong, because a feed stopped refreshing three days ago or a join started dropping rows, and nothing in the stack was built to care.

In most industries that is an embarrassing dashboard. In banking it can turn into a regulatory submission, a liquidity figure in front of a risk committee, or a customer statement. The stakes shift quite a lot. So this piece is about silent failures: what they look like, why banks are unusually exposed to them, and a way of building observability that catches them before a report breaks. I should say early that it will not catch everything. I'll come back to what it misses.

I can think of three reasons, though there are probably more.

First, the chains are long. A single regulatory figure, say a liquidity coverage ratio, might pass through a core banking extract, a treasury system, a reference data service, a staging layer, a transformation layer and finally a reporting tool. Each hop belongs to someone else, often with a release calendar nobody downstream has seen.

Second, banks lean heavily on batch. Plenty of critical feeds arrive once a day, and some only once a month. If a daily feed breaks on Tuesday, you might not see the damage until the Friday reconciliation, or the month-end close. A long feedback loop gives bad data plenty of time to travel.

Third, and this is the uncomfortable one, a lot of existing monitoring answers the question "did the job run?" when the question that matters is "is the data right?" Those are different questions. A job can run perfectly and load nothing at all.

None of the following is a real incident from a named bank, but the shapes are familiar to anyone who has worked near a data warehouse.

The stale rate table. An FX rates feed from a market data vendor stops updating after a change on the vendor side. Your pipeline keeps reading the table, which still has plenty of rows, so the job-level check passes. Euro and dollar positions get converted at last Wednesday's rate. Totals look sensible. They just are not true.

The shrinking join. An upstream team changes a code in a product reference table, perhaps a new product type with no mapping yet. An inner join quietly drops everything that no longer matches. Three percent of the loan book disappears from a report. Three percent does not look dramatic on a chart. In a capital calculation, it might be very dramatic.

The drifting distribution. A source system starts defaulting a null field, like days past due, to zero. Row counts are identical. The schema is identical. But the share of loans classed as current jumps overnight, and nobody changed a credit policy.

None of these throws an exception. All of them pass a "job succeeded" check.

I'm a bit wary of the word "observability" because vendors have stretched it until it covers almost anything. The distinction I find useful is simple. Monitoring checks things you already know can go wrong. Observability means collecting enough information about the data itself, continuously, that when something strange happens you can work out where it started and what it touched.

For data, that mostly means watching the data and not only the machinery. CPU on the warehouse tells you very little about whether the FX table is current.

There are lots of ways to slice this. The five below are the ones I keep coming back to, partly because each maps neatly to one of the failures above.

Freshness. When did this table last change, compared with when it should have? One trap here: check the business date inside the data, not the load timestamp. A job can load yesterday's rates today and look perfectly fresh by the wrong clock. That is exactly how the stale rate table slips through.

Volume. Are row counts in a plausible range? The word that matters is plausible, because banks have calendars. UK bank holidays, month-end, quarter-end and year-end all change expected volumes. A check that ignores them will cry wolf every few weeks, and people will stop listening.

Schema. Have columns been added, dropped or retyped? This is the cheapest signal to collect and often the most useful, since a renamed column is a common cause of everything downstream going subtly wrong.

Distribution. Null rates, value ranges, category proportions, and sums of balances. This is where the drifting distribution gets caught. It is also the noisiest signal, so I would introduce it last.

Lineage. Which reports depend on this table? When a check fails, lineage tells you the blast radius. Without it, the alert reads "something is odd in staging" and everyone shrugs. With it, the alert reads "something is odd in staging, and it feeds the liquidity report due at 10am". That is a very different conversation.

Here is the layout I would sketch on a whiteboard. The main idea is that checks live at the boundaries between layers, not only at the end next to the report.

Reading it left to right, the data moves from source systems through ingestion, raw storage, staging, curated marts, and finally the regulatory and management reports. Underneath, an observability layer attaches a different kind of check to each stage.

At ingestion, you ask the cheap questions: did the file arrive, is it fresh by business date, does the schema match the agreed contract? In staging, you look at keys, referential integrity and null rates. In the marts, you run reconciliations and distribution checks. At the report layer, you compare control totals against the prior period and against the general ledger.

Reconciliation deserves a special mention because it is old-fashioned and brilliant. Finance teams have done it for decades. The idea is that the sum of balances in your mart should equal the sum in the source extract, within a tolerance. If a join drops three percent of the loan book, a control total notices immediately, even though row counts and schemas look fine. Plenty of data teams skip it because it feels unglamorous. I would start there.

Every check writes its result to a metadata store. That store feeds the alerting layer and, ideally, a lineage graph, so a failure can be traced to the reports it threatens.

A small example of the volume check, written as plain SQL so it is easy to port. It compares the latest day against the same weekday over the past eight weeks. Treat it as a sketch rather than production code, because it knows nothing about holidays yet.

If the z-score goes past something like 3, raise a flag. The threshold is a guess you will tune, and you should expect to be wrong about it the first few times.

Collecting signals is the easy half. The harder half is making sure a human reacts to them.

I have seen, or at least heard enough war stories to believe in, the pattern where a team switches on two hundred checks, gets forty alerts a day, and within a month has muted the channel. At that point you have built an expensive way of generating noise. So the design question is less "what can we check?" and more "what deserves to interrupt someone?"

A scheme that tends to hold up has three tiers. Informational checks get logged and reviewed weekly. Warnings go to the named owner of the dataset during working hours. Critical failures, meaning anything that touches a regulatory report, go to the owner immediately and also close a gate in front of the publish step.

That gate is the controversial part. Some teams prefer to publish anyway with a visible warning banner, on the argument that a late report is worse than a flagged one. Others hold the previous approved version until someone signs off. I lean towards holding for regulatory outputs and warning for internal dashboards, but I can see the other side. If your submission deadline is fixed by a regulator, the calculation changes.

Whichever way you go, two things matter more than the tooling. Every dataset needs a named owner, a person and not a shared inbox. And upstream teams need a lightweight data contract, even a one-page agreement, saying which columns and codes they promise not to change without notice. Without that, you are monitoring someone else's decisions with no way to influence them.

I would be overselling it if I stopped there.

Observability catches data that is stale, missing, malformed or oddly distributed. It does not catch data that is fresh, complete, consistent and simply wrong because the business logic misreads a rule. A risk weight applied to the wrong asset class will sail through every check described above. That needs code review, testing and domain experts, and no dashboard replaces them.

Thresholds can also create false confidence. A check tuned so loosely that it never fires is worse than no check, because people assume it is protecting them. Anomaly detection tools driven by machine learning can help with tuning, but I am slightly cautious about them in a regulated setting. An auditor can read a rule that says "volume within three standard deviations of the weekday baseline". A black box that quietly adapts its own thresholds is harder to defend.

And then there is the organisational side, which no architecture diagram captures. If upstream teams see your alerts as an accusation and not a courtesy, the checks will be ignored. A bit of diplomacy goes a long way here.

If I were starting on Monday, I would not try to cover the whole warehouse. I would pick one regulatory report, trace its lineage back to the ten or so tables it truly depends on, and add three things: freshness by business date, a volume check with a calendar, and a control total that reconciles to source.

Then I would assign owners and run everything in warn-only mode for two weeks. That gives you a feel for false positives before anyone is woken up at night. Only after that would I switch the critical checks to blocking.

That staged approach is slower than a big-bang rollout, and some teams will find it frustrating. But it builds trust in the alerts, and trust is the thing that decides whether anyone responds when the real one fires.

Silent failures are hard because they look like success. The pipeline is green, the report is on time, and the number is wrong. Catching them means shifting attention from whether the job ran to whether the data still makes sense, and doing it at every boundary, not just at the finish line.

None of this is exotic. Freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage, plus a few reconciliations that finance has trusted for decades. The hard parts are the unglamorous ones: ownership, contracts, tuning thresholds and keeping the noise low enough that people still care. If your team is working through the same problem, I would be curious which of the five signals you found most useful in practice. My bet is freshness by business date, but I could easily be wrong.

The Missing Layer in Enterprise AI: A Governance Architecture for LLMs and Machine Learning

#9787. Flowise Chatflow API Keys Do Not Boundary the Stored Credentials

A Flowise chatflow can be protected by an API key and still execute nodes that use stored third-party credentials. The key controls who can call the flow, not what secrets the flow can reach. A review that stops at the public endpoint misses the credential store, the node permissions, and the external systems the flow can access.

Flowise documentation describes chatflow-level authorization with a generated API key and an Authorization header. It also states that an unauthenticated public chatflow API or embedded chat can be accessed by anyone. The environment documentation says Flowise encrypts third-party API keys as credentials using an encryption key, and SECRETKEY_PATH controls where the secret key is stored.

The first zone is the person or application calling the chatflow. The second is the running flow, including tools, HTTP nodes, vector stores, and model providers. The third is the credential store and its encryption key. An API key in the first zone should not imply access to the third.

Inventory each flow's exposed endpoint, authentication setting, allowed users, and external integrations. Identify which credential IDs it references without printing the secret values. Limit the flow's ability to call arbitrary HTTP endpoints or shell tools unless that capability is reviewed.

Store SECRETKEY_PATH on persistent protected storage with restricted filesystem permissions. Back it up separately from the database and test restoration. If an attacker obtains both the encrypted credential database and the encryption key, the UI length difference for a credential API key does not provide protection.

Rotate the encryption strategy through a planned migration, not by replacing the key in place without a re-encryption process. Confirm that worker and web processes use the same key and that a restart does not create a new key without the operator noticing.

An embedded chat or public API may be a legitimate front door. Add authentication at the reverse proxy or application layer when the flow can spend money, query private data, or call internal systems. Apply rate limits, request-size limits, timeout controls, and output filters. Log the flow ID and caller identity without logging complete prompts that may contain personal data.

Test whether a chatflow API key can be used against another flow. Test an unauthenticated request to each public and private path. Check CORS, cache headers, and whether the browser exposes the key in client-side code.

The count-only measurement used sub_type=all, page 1, and page size 1. app="Flowise" returned 40,899, title="Flowise" returned 42,439, and http.body="Flowise" returned 485,939. The body count is large and can include documentation, examples, and unrelated references. A public Flowise fingerprint is a discovery lead, not proof that a credential is exposed or that a flow is exploitable.

Correlate owned instances with cloud tags, DNS, certificate names, and expected business units. If a development instance is public by mistake, disable its external access before investigating individual flows.

Create a flow inventory with owner, purpose, external credentials, data sources, and endpoint authorization. Review it when a new tool node is added, not only at deployment. The security boundary is the combination of caller identity, flow capability, and secret access.

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9782. Monthly Instagram Reports for SMM Clients

It was the last working day of the month, the day I send my clients their Instagram reports. I had a coffee, a half-finished report and a script that had worked fine the previous month. Then it died on a login challenge, and I spent the next hour re-authenticating an account instead of sending anything. I'm a freelance social media manager who writes just enough Python to get into trouble, and that hour was when I started asking whether I should be maintaining this at all.

Once a month I pull stats for each client's account (followers, recent posts, how the posts did) and turn them into a report. The volume is small, but the deadline is real and the numbers have to be right, because clients read them.

I used instagrapi first, and I'd still recommend it in the right situation. It's free, it's well maintained, and it gives you a lot of control. For a hobby project or a one-off script it's hard to beat.

None of that is the library's fault. It's how that approach works.

I moved the collection step to HikerAPI, a hosted REST API. You send your key in an x-access-key header and call an endpoint. It's pay-per-request, starting at about $0.001 per request, and there are 100 free requests to try it. I used those to compare the output with what I see in the app before changing anything.

That's the whole login flow: there isn't one. My report script went from managing sessions and retries to looping over a list of usernames and saving each response to a file, so a failed run only re-fetches what's missing.

For my use, small and deadline-driven, the hosted API removed the part that kept breaking. If you're a developer who enjoys controlling every layer, or you run a lot of accounts yourself, instagrapi may still be the better fit.

Disclosure: the provider offers free credits for write-ups like this one, so weigh my opinion accordingly. The comparison above comes from what I actually ran into.

What's your setup for recurring Instagram reports? Still running your own, or have you handed it off?

Melbourne, Florida, November 5th, 2026/CyberNewswire/--OpenMatter Network, a pioneer in decentralized infrastructure for agentic artificial intelligence, is positioning its decentralized computing platform as an alternative to massive, centralized data center development amid growing public opposition to new facilities.

The company says its approach can support continued AI adoption by enabling computing workloads to run across distributed resources rather than relying primarily on large-scale data center infrastructure.

The results of Tuesday's midterm elections have put growing public opposition to massive data center development in the national spotlight. However, according to OpenMatter Network, resistance to new facilities need not signal a slowdown in AI adoption. Instead, it could accelerate the transition to a computing model that reduces dependence on massive, centralized data centers.

“Voters have made it clear that they are increasingly concerned about the enormous energy demands, environmental impact and rising utility costs associated with massive data center development,” said Mike Anderson, CEO of OpenMatter Network. “But the need to deploy agentic AI isn’t going away. Businesses don’t have to choose between advancing AI and addressing these very legitimate concerns. There is another path forward, and OpenMatter is helping make it possible.”

Across the country, communities have expressed concerns about the impact of large-scale facilities on electricity rates, water supplies, local infrastructure and the environment. The election has brought renewed attention to those concerns and the policy choices surrounding new construction.

“The assumption that AI must be built around increasingly massive concentrations of computing power deserves to be challenged,” Anderson continued. “Our decentralized architecture allows computing resources to be distributed across many different locations. That means organizations have another way to move forward with agentic AI as communities and policymakers reconsider the costs and consequences of building more enormous data centers.”

The OpenMatter Network platform is designed to transform widely available computing hardware into usable network resources through its distributed architecture, algorithms and verifiable computing capabilities. By enabling independently owned computing resources to participate in a shared network, OpenMatter is working to make decentralized infrastructure a practical alternative for enterprise AI deployment.

“There’s an enormous amount of computing capacity outside the walls of traditional data centers,” said Renee Davis, co-founder and chief business officer of OpenMatter Network. “Our technology makes it possible to bring those resources together in a verifiable network capable of supporting real-world AI workloads. Rather than concentrating computing power in a relatively small number of massive facilities, we can distribute workloads across existing resources and smaller installations, creating opportunities for a more flexible and potentially more energy-efficient approach to AI infrastructure.”

The decentralized model also offers organizations greater flexibility in where computing resources are located and how they are deployed. This can be particularly valuable for businesses and government institutions seeking greater control over computing infrastructure, including those with requirements for data sovereignty and locally managed resources.

“The question is no longer simply how many more massive data centers we need to build,” Anderson concluded. “It’s how we can deploy the AI capabilities businesses need without imposing unnecessary burdens on the communities where computing resources are located. Tuesday’s election results make that question more urgent than ever. OpenMatter offers a new way forward.”

Headquartered in Florida’s Space Coast, OpenMatter Network is building the Verifiable Trust Layer for Secure Collaboration and AI Agents. Guided by the principle “Don’t Trust Data. Prove It.,” the company’s cryptographically verifiable architecture enables secure collaboration, governed AI behavior and mathematically verifiable execution across untrusted environments. For more information, visit www.openmatter.network.

#9779. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

#9775. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9774. Order Beats Randomness: Bisecting Test Pollution in Agent Patches

Most tests labeled "flaky" in an agent-patch pipeline are not nondeterministic at all. They are order-dependent: they pass alone, and fail after some other test leaves shared state behind. Randomization masks that. Bisection names it.

The distinction matters because the two failures have opposite remedies. A genuinely random failure earns a temporary freeze. An order-dependent failure earns a fixture fix — and freezing it instead quietly locks in a bug that resurfaces the next time an agent inserts a file.

What follows is a reproduction-first workflow: prove the target passes alone, delta-debug the smallest prefix that breaks it, then classify the result before anyone touches a quarantine list.

Agents insert files. Runners collect files in a fixed order, usually alphabetical by path. An agent that adds tests/test_auth_refresh.py next to an existing tests/test_z_session.py changes execution order for everything in between, without editing a single existing test.

Session-scoped fixtures are the usual carrier: a cache, a temp database, an env var, a module-level client. The new first test warms it in a way the old second test does not expect.

Then the pipeline sees test_rotate fail at head, pass at base, and pass when re-run alone. The label "flaky" follows. That label is close to meaningless — the test never was nondeterministic, the schedule changed.

Before bisecting, prove the target passes in isolation, repeatedly, at head.

Three outcomes, and only one of them belongs in this workflow:

-p no:randomly disables the plugin if your suite uses one. Without it, the isolation run and the pollution run are not comparable, and the whole exercise produces noise.

Now find the smallest set of tests that, run before the target in their original order, still makes the target fail. Shrinking matters: a 400-test prefix is not usable evidence in a review comment.

Run it against the failing target and the suite root:

Illustrative output on a suite where a new file landed ahead of an older one:

The predicate is order-preserving on purpose. You are not asking whether the two tests are related. You are asking whether this schedule is sufficient. Reordering the minimized subset afterwards is a separate and useful follow-up: if the pair fails in either order, you have shared global state, not a directional dependency.

Do not act on the bisection result until it lands in a row of this table.

Only row 3 earns a freeze. Rows 1 and 2 are test bugs with a named owner, and they cost a fixture edit rather than a suppression entry. Mixing the rows is how quarantine lists grow monotonically while suite reliability stays flat.

Whatever you conclude, write it next to the test. A suppression marker with no reason is an invitation for the next agent to "fix" it by deleting the test.

Two properties make this note useful: a named issue, and a stated removal condition. A freeze without an exit condition is a permanent deletion with extra steps.

The bisection is cheap per target but embarrassingly parallel across targets — every node ID in a failing run is a candidate root cause. That is a short-lived, bursty workload rather than a steady one, which is the shape a free server option handles well. It is why I ran this batch step on MonkeyCode's free server: the machine only needs to exist for the length of a triage pass, then it can go away.

The model side is the second half. Sorting a minimized prefix into the table above is a reading task — does the polluting test touch a session fixture, an env var, a module-level cache, a temp path? Drafting that first pass across dozens of prefixes is well within what free model access handles, and a human then confirms it by reading the two tests side by side. Treat the draft as a hypothesis generator, not a verdict.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The gate is not "is this test flaky." The gate is "can I name the test that breaks it." Only one of those questions has an answer you can paste into a review comment.

#9773. Gate Pioneers Proof of Security, Achieving 104.58% Cold Storage Coverage to Solidify Asset Security

We're your all-in-one marketing hub tailored for the crypto and blockchain sectors.

We're your all-in-one marketing hub tailored for the crypto and blockchain sectors.

We're your all-in-one marketing hub tailored for the crypto and blockchain sectors.

Gate has officially introduced Proof of Security (PoSEC), a new asset security verification framework, becoming the first digital asset trading platform in the industry to launch a PoSEC security verification system. Since its founding in 2013, Gate has consistently placed user asset security at the forefront of its priorities.

With the introduction of PoSEC, Gate extends security verification beyond reserve adequacy to include asset storage structures and risk coverage capabilities, further solidifying safeguards for user assets and providing a new practical approach to advancing industry security standards.

Unlike Proof of Reserves (PoR), which primarily verifies the adequacy of asset reserves, PoSEC places additional emphasis on asset storage security. By publicly disclosing the distribution of assets between platform cold storage and hot wallets, PoSEC provides visibility into asset storage structures and their ability to cover potential losses under extreme scenarios.

PoSEC introduces the cold storage coverage ratio as a key metric to measure the extent to which cold storage covers total user assets. A coverage ratio ≥ 100% means that, under the applicable calculation methodology, cold storage alone would be sufficient to cover all user assets even if all assets held in hot wallets were lost. PoR and PoSEC serve complementary purposes, extending asset security verification from reserve adequacy to storage security and risk coverage, while providing users with more comprehensive and transparent information about asset security.

According to the snapshot taken at 00:00 (UTC) on November 4, 2026, Gate's cold storage coverage ratio reached 104.58%, with cold storage and hot wallet assets accounting for 88.26% and 11.74% of total assets, respectively. Cold storage assets include digital assets held offline and traditional assets under independent custody. To qualify, these assets must meet requirements such as not being directly used for routine deposits and withdrawals, being held offline or under independent custody, requiring multi-party authorization for transfers, and being independently verifiable.

The current data is undergoing verification by an independent third-party audit firm. The review covers asset authenticity and control, valuation and calculation methodologies, and coverage ratio calculations. The audit report will be published on Gate's official website upon completion, enhancing the transparency and credibility of asset security disclosures.

Gate has long been committed to digital asset security and transparency. In 2020, Gate was among the first in the industry to introduce an open-source Proof of Reserves (PoR) mechanism and a Merkle Tree-based asset verification solution, establishing itself as an early contributor to reserve transparency in the industry. Gate subsequently incorporated technologies such as zk-SNARKs to enhance its asset reserve verification framework.

As of October 18, 2026, Gate's total reserves amounted to approximately $8.688 billion, with an overall reserve ratio of 118.49%. The platform also employs a range of security mechanisms, including hot and cold wallet segregation, multi-signature technology, Multi-Party Computation (MPC), dynamic risk monitoring, and zero-trust access control, to establish a multi-layered security framework covering asset reserves, storage management, and risk protection.

From PoR, which verifies reserve adequacy, to PoSEC, which verifies asset storage security and risk coverage capabilities, Gate is progressively building a multi-layered security framework encompassing asset reserves, storage management, risk protection, and public verification. Looking ahead, Gate will continue to uphold its security-first principle, further develop PoSEC standards and verification mechanisms, and collaborate with more industry participants to enhance asset security and transparency, laying a stronger security foundation for the long-term, sustainable development of the digital asset industry.

Learn more:

Gate, founded in 2013 by Dr. Han, is one of the world's leading cryptocurrency and integrated financial services platforms, spanning financial and everyday use cases including asset management, trading and payments. Serving over 62 million users globally, it supports trading across 5,400+ digital assets and 12,800+ stock assets and ETFs, while providing access to a comprehensive range of TradFi assets, including metals, stocks, indices, forex, and commodities to meet users' end-to-end needs across asset holding, trading, and spending. As an industry benchmark, Gate was among the first platforms to implement 100% Proof of Reserves. Its ecosystem includes Gate Money, Gate Wallet, Gate Ventures, Gate for AI Agent, and a wide range of products and services.

#9771. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.
