#9770. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9768. Your client paid you less than the invoice. Here's where the money went (and how to get it back)

If you freelance for companies in India, Indonesia, the Philippines, Spain, most of Latin America, parts of Africa, or you do construction work in the UK, you have probably had this moment: you invoice 2,000, and 1,800 lands in your account. No dispute, no late fee, no explanation.

The missing 200 is withholding tax (also called tax deducted at source, retención, PPh, TDS, CIS, or in the US "backup withholding"). Your client was legally required to keep part of your fee and pay it to the tax office in your name. It is not a cost — it is a prepayment of your own income tax. But it only counts as a prepayment if you can prove it. Most freelancers can't, so they pay the tax twice.

This post is the bookkeeping system I use to make sure that never happens, plus the spreadsheet logic so you can build it yourself.

The core mistake is tracking only the invoice total. Every invoice actually has three amounts you care about:

In a spreadsheet, with the fee in F, withholding rate in H and the sales-tax toggle in Settings:

Note the order: withholding is usually calculated on the pre-tax fee, and sales tax is added on top of it. If your country does it the other way, it's a one-cell change — but write the rule down once and apply it to every invoice, because a tracker that is inconsistent is worse than none.

Rates change. Clients also fall into categories (business with your tax ID on file, business without it, private individual, overseas). Put the categories and their rates in one small table and let every invoice look them up:

where column G is a dropdown of the type names. When your country's rate changes from 10% to 12%, you edit one cell and every invoice that uses that type updates. If you had typed 10% into 80 rows, you now have 80 edits and probably three mistakes.

A small discipline that pays off: keep NONE (0%) as the first row. Private clients and most overseas clients don't withhold, and "no type selected" should mean zero, not an error.

Here is what actually recovers the money. Your tax return lets you claim withheld tax as a credit, but the tax office will only accept it with the client's withholding certificate (Form 16A in India, bukti potong in Indonesia, CIS statement in the UK, etc.). Clients forget. You forget. By filing season it's a scramble.

So the tracker has one column on the invoice sheet — Certificate received? YES / NO / N/A — and a separate sheet that lists only the invoices with withholding, pulled automatically:

Then two numbers at the top of that sheet:

The second number is your to-do list. Chase it monthly, when the client's finance team still remembers the payment, not in April.

Now every dashboard number is a SUMIFS on those columns, with a <>CANCELLED guard so voided invoices never inflate revenue:

Twelve rows for months, four rows for quarters (sum of three months each), and you have: invoices issued, revenue, sales tax collected (this is your VAT return), tax withheld (this is your credit), net cash billed, cash received, outstanding. The quarterly block exists for estimated / advance tax payments, which most countries base on the quarter's actual income.

One more column I always add: suggested set-aside = cash received × a percentage you choose (I use 25%). It's not a tax computation, it's a nudge to move money into a separate account before it turns into a new lens.

A due date is just invoice date + terms. Days late depends on status:

Paid: how late was the payment. Unpaid: how late is it right now. Cancelled: zero. Add a conditional-format rule — red fill when P > 0 and status isn't PAID — and your receivables list reads itself. The dashboard KPIs then come free: overdue total, overdue count, average days to payment (AVERAGEIFS of P on paid invoices + terms), collection rate (cash received ÷ net cash billed).

You don't need an invoicing app for a clean invoice. One sheet, one yellow cell for the invoice number, and every field is:

Show subtotal, sales tax, total, then — and this is what clients appreciate — a line that says "Less tax withheld at source (WHT 10%): −200" and "Amount payable: 1,800". When the invoice already shows the net amount, nobody at the client's end has to guess, and you get far fewer "we paid what the invoice said" arguments.

That's the system: three amounts per invoice, rates in a lookup table, a certificate log, month/quarter helpers, status-aware lateness, and a print sheet. It takes about an evening to build from scratch.

If you'd rather not spend the evening, I packaged exactly this as a 7-sheet Excel workbook (5,700 live formulas, no macros, works in Excel / Google Sheets / LibreOffice, every rate is an input so it fits any country): Freelancer Invoice & Tax Tracker 2026 — English edition, $9. Indonesian freelancers: the bilingual edition with PPh 23 / PPh 21 / PPN pre-wired is here.

#9766. Draft Only What a Probe Can Fail: A Section Ownership Ledger for Model-Written Docs

Split documentation at the point where a claim can be falsified by a command. Everything on the machine-checkable side of that line may be drafted by a model; everything on the other side needs a named human author, not a reviewer. This post turns that rule into two small scripts and a tab-separated ledger you can run in CI.

Most doc-generation failures I have seen are not hallucinated sentences. They are correctly written sentences about a surface that changed, sitting in a section nobody was assigned to own. A reviewer checkbox does not fix that, because reviewing prose is cheap and owning a fact is expensive. The ledger makes the ownership explicit and makes the split mechanical.

A section is model-draftable only when it satisfies three conditions at once. Its factual content must be extractable from a program (CLI help text, config schema, HTTP headers, exit codes). Every number in the drafted prose must appear in that extracted bundle. And it must carry zero unresolved judgment claims, meaning no sentence of the form "you should prefer X because Y".

Everything else is human-owned. That includes migration advice, security guarantees, deprecation rationale, performance expectations, and any statement about intent. Those sections are not reviewed by a human after drafting; they are written by a human and merely proofread by whoever is available.

The split is worth doing because the two failure modes have different costs. A stale flag table wastes a reader's afternoon. A wrong migration recommendation wastes a reader's week.

Create docplan.tsv next to your docs directory. Five columns, tab-separated, one row per section. The probe column points at a test file relative to the plan; handwritten_claims counts the judgment statements you already know the section needs.

The important column is handwritten_claims. It is a declaration that this section contains sentences no probe can produce, and it forces the row into the human bucket. If a section starts at 0 and later grows judgment content, the count changes and the gate re-files it.

The gate does not know whether the docs are true. It only enforces that the plan is coherent and that every model-drafted section has a probe file that actually exists. That is enough to catch the common failure where a section is marked model-draftable and the test was deleted six weeks ago.

Run it as python3 ownership_gate.py docplan.tsv. On the table above it prints sections=5 model=3 human=2 and exits zero. Rename a probe file and it exits one with a line-pointer and the missing path.

Each probe writes a JSON bundle of the facts it can observe. The model receives the bundle and nothing else as a source of numbers. Keeping the bundle plain text matters: it makes the input diffable, so a reviewer can see that the flag list shrank by two entries this week.

This is also where a hosted environment saves time. MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are operator-supplied availability claims, and they are relevant here in a narrow way: the drafting loop and the probe pipeline can both run on a throwaway machine instead of on the laptop that holds your credentials.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

A model can produce a fluent section that cites a real fact bundle and still misattribute a number, for example by pairing a timeout value with the wrong endpoint. The audit is deliberately narrow: it checks only that every numeral in the drafted section appears somewhere in that section's bundle. It cannot catch misattribution, which is why step 5 exists.

Call it per section: python3 fact_audit.py .docfacts/probe_cli.json docs/cli-flags.md. The exit code is the gate. A section that reports unbacked=0 is not correct; it is merely anchored.

Use this table when you are unsure which side of the line a section belongs on. The right column is not a review duty; it is authorship.

The most useful behaviour of this pipeline is that it does not fill the judgment sections. The generator writes stubs/migration-guide.md containing the four declared claims as open questions and the owning handle, and CI fails while those files are missing. The model never touches them, which removes the temptation to accept a plausible paragraph because it arrived on time.

That is the whole discipline: the model is fast where a test can disagree with it, and silent where only a person can.

Probe existence is not probe quality, so a probe that always emits an empty bundle will pass the gate and produce hollow docs. The numeric audit catches invented figures and nothing else, meaning wrong pairings of real facts survive it. The ledger also cannot verify that the named owner read anything, so treat the handle as an accountability statement rather than proof of work.

Finally, do not wire a free tier into a release-blocking path as a permanent assumption. Availability, model behaviour, and limits can change without notice; keep a fallback where the three machine sections are generated from the fact bundle by a local template when the drafting step is unavailable.

Skip the ledger if your documentation is primarily positioning, tutorials, or narrative explanation, because almost every section lands in the human bucket and the plan becomes paperwork. Skip it if your repository has no executable surface to probe, or if the docs change less often than the ledger itself would. Teams of one or two may also find the tab-separated file heavier than a single OWNERS note in the README.

If you want to try it, the two scripts above are the entire dependency list; start by classifying five existing sections and see how many survive as model-draftable.

#9765. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9761. Paper 5: What survives when the model, client, and machine change?

A model session ending should not mean that the system forgets who is authorized, what is in scope, what evidence supports a record, or how an earlier decision can be audited.

That sounds obvious—until you ask where those things actually live.

If they live only in a live prompt, a model’s context window, a particular client, or the memory of one running process, then they are not really system continuity. They are temporary convenience.

My fifth preprint, The Continuity Substrate, tests a different proposition: can governed operational continuity survive changes in models, clients, machines, operating systems, and runtime restarts when the continuity contract is maintained outside the inference session?

The answer from this controlled study is narrow but encouraging.

Under named first-party synthetic conditions, the governed substrate preserved its deterministic contract across:

The point is not that any model has become magically permanent. It has not.

The point is that important continuity should not be entrusted to a model session in the first place.

In this architecture, models can change. Clients can change. A runtime can restart. The intelligence can come and go. What must remain stable—authority, scope, provenance, consent, auditability, and the rules for releasing information—belongs in a governed substrate outside inference.

That matters for ordinary software as much as it matters for AI. If someone changes providers, upgrades a model, moves from one device to another, or restarts a service, they should not have to negotiate their digital history from scratch. And they should never discover that a new model has quietly inherited information it was not authorized to see.

There are real limits to this paper. It does not claim production readiness, security certification, universal portability, or independent replication. It reports a controlled test and a public evidence package so readers can inspect the boundary being claimed.

But it asks a question I think the industry needs to take more seriously:

When the intelligence changes, where does the responsibility stay?

Read the open preprint and inspect the public evidence package here:

The model may be brilliant. But continuity, permission, and accountability should not disappear when the model closes its eyes.

#9758. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

Get more tips for holiday success in our Thanksgiving Baking Guide.

#9757. A Passing Characterization Test Proves Nothing Until You Break the Code

Most characterization tests in a messy repo are decoration. They pass before the refactor. They pass after it. They would also pass if the branch under test were deleted.

That is not a test. It is a receipt. This post adds one cheap gate: prove each new test can fail, by breaking the code on purpose.

A vacuous test usually appears during refactor prep. Someone snapshots a return value. Or writes assert result is not None. It goes green, the team feels safe, and the gate stays open.

Then the refactor changes rounding, ordering, or a default. The suite stays green. The bug ships. The test was never guarding the seam you touched.

Coverage does not catch this. A line can execute and still be unobserved. The only honest question is: which code change makes this test fail?

Adopt a single rule for refactor prep. Every new characterization test must kill at least one deliberate mutation.

A mutation is a tiny, mechanical edit to the source. Change >= to > — swap a default — drop a rounding call. If the test still passes, the test cannot see that behavior.

Keep the mutant set small and hand-written. You are guarding a seam, not scoring the whole file.

Refactors fail at boundaries, not at file scope. Name the boundary before you write anything: a function, a public method, a serialized payload.

Write that name down. Also write the caller that must keep working. If you cannot name the caller, you are not ready to refactor.

Mutation results are worthless when the test is random. Pin time, IDs, and env reads behind module-level functions you can patch.

Run the target test five times in a row. If any run differs, stop. Fix determinism before you fix anything else.

Run the current code and record what it actually produces. Not what you believe it should produce. Paste that output into the assertion.

Ugly golden values are fine here. They are temporary scaffolding for the diff. You delete or re-derive them after the behavior is documented.

List the edits that would break a caller without crashing. Boundaries, defaults, rounding, and ordering are the usual suspects.

Keep them as data, not as a tool config. Two to six entries per seam is enough.

Each mutant must match exactly once. A pattern that matches zero or three times is a broken mutant, not a survived one.

The runner copies the repo, applies one mutant, runs one test node, then restores the file. Classify the exit code honestly.

Exit code 5 deserves attention. It means the selector matched no tests, which silently poisons the whole gate.

Survivors split into two kinds. Real gaps get a tighter assertion. Equivalent mutants — edits with no observable behavior change — should be deleted from the list, not chased.

Writing mutants by hand is fast. Finding the seams you forgot is not. A model is decent at proposing candidate assertions and candidate mutants for unfamiliar code.

Give it the function and the callers. Ask for boundary inputs and, for each input, the one-line edit that should change the output. Then run the loop.

The loop is the judge. A model proposal that kills nothing is dropped, no matter how plausible the reasoning sounds. Free model access on MonkeyCode is enough for this propose-then-verify pattern, since the artifact is text, not a passing test suite. The same loop runs fine on a remote machine; MonkeyCode's free server option is one place to park it if you would rather not pin a laptop core. Check the current quotas and limits yourself — free tiers change without notice.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Now edit production code. One seam per commit. Then re-run the exact same mutant set.

The kill set must be identical before and after. New kills mean you changed behavior nobody asked for. Lost kills mean the test stopped guarding the seam.

That comparison is the gate. It is also cheaper than reviewing a large diff by eye.

Start with one module and one seam. Run the loop once. Count the survivors before you write any new test.

That count is your real starting point for the refactor.

#9752. 51 Thanksgiving dessert recipes for a sweet holiday: From cookies to cake — and of course, plenty of pie.

Of course, we had to start with pumpkin pie. This is a rich, well-spiced pie, thanks to a powerful punch of ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper. Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

With its retro vibe, this play on classic chiffon pie is noteworthy for its tender rye crust and its bright, light chiffon filling. The zesty cranberry curd and smooth, sweet Swiss meringue play beautifully together. And the gelatin helps the filling set just right so that once refrigerated, the pie can be sliced neatly. Tart and airy, this pie is an excellent counterpoint to a heavy feast.

Shop the recipe: Organic Medium Rye Flour

Intimidated by pie? Don't be! Our guide on How to Bake Pie has everything you need for a successful, stress-free bake.

This double-crusted beauty is generously filled with sweet-tart apples and spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg, and allspice. But the real secret to its flavorful filling is boiled cider, one of our favorite fall ingredients. The sticky tart-sweet syrup adds an extra depth of apple flavor to make this classic pie stand out from the crowd.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Boiled Cider and Instant ClearJel

This unusual method for baking apple pie caught our eye years ago, when a reader sent it via e-mail. But it’s not just a stunt: Baking a pie in a paper grocery bag gives you a beautifully golden brown, perfectly cooked pie, with toothsome yet tender apples (which soften better thanks to the steam trapped by the bag) beneath a streusel topping.

This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. Top it with toasted molasses meringue (if you want the pie to be reminiscent of the classic yams and marshmallow dish served at Thanksgiving), or for a simpler option, with freshly whipped cream. (And for a more unconventional version, try this striking Purple Sweet Potato Pie.)

This traditional pie doesn’t use corn syrup — instead, it’s sweetened entirely with brown sugar. The filling is silky smooth, and the pecans on top toast nicely as the pie bakes. Be sure to use high-quality vanilla extract for well-rounded flavor; an optional handful of chopped bittersweet chocolate is a nice addition, too.

If you’re intimidated by pie (or just don’t have time to chill and roll out pie dough) this easier version of pecan pie is for you. A buttery, brown-sugar shortbread crust cradles a gooey honey-sweetened pecan filling. These bars keep well for days, so they’re perfect for baking ahead of Thanksgiving.

This recipe takes classic pecan pie a step further by adding chocolate chips to the filling. The chocolate beautifully complements the pecans' nuttiness; if you choose bittersweet chocolate, it cuts the pie's overall sweetness, allowing all of the flavors to shine more brightly.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Bittersweet Chocolate Chips

Baker's tip: Make and freeze your pie crust early to get ahead on pie prep.

This creamy, decadent pie is positively bursting with maple flavor — be sure to use the best maple syrup you can find and a dash of natural maple flavor to enhance it. One bite of the brûléed maple sugar top and the silky-smooth filling will have you reconsidering your regular rotation of cream pies this Thanksgiving.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar. If you’re only in charge of dessert this year and want to flex a little, this recipe is an impressive (and tasty!) way to do so.

Shop the recipe: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

Mash-up pies are an easy way to please your guests without making multiple pies. This recipe has the best of both worlds: a smooth layer of spiced pumpkin custard plus a rich pecan topping. It’s best made a day ahead so that the flavors can settle, plus there’s one less dish to worry about on Thanksgiving Day.

Shop the recipe: Adjustable Pie Crust Shield

Is there anything cuter than a mini Thanksgiving pie? Filled with a pre-cooked, perfectly spiced filling that’s enhanced with tart boiled cider, these bite-sized treats can be topped with a woven lattice or streusel.

This tart-sweet cake is easy to throw together — made with melted butter, the one-bowl batter is mixed by hand then poured directly over sugared cranberries. If you have cranberries leftover from making sauce or just want to highlight these seasonal berries in other ways, make this cake.

This stunning pumpkin swirl cake is more than just good looks: It also has a soft, plush texture, thanks to cake flour and sour cream, and a deep pumpkin flavor paired with fragrant vanilla. It starts with one base batter that gets flavored two ways, creating two distinct colors for a striking visual contrast when sliced.

For a more traditional dessert, try this pumpkin-y layer cake. It’s moist and slightly dense from the pumpkin purée, with a tangy cream cheese frosting and sticky caramel glaze.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

In this unabashedly apple-forward apple cake, there are so many apple slices and so little batter, you’ll wonder how (and if) it will hold together. But never fear: As the batter rises in the oven, it knits those slices together to create a tender cake that’s almost creamy and custardy due to the abundance of fruit.

Shop the recipe: Almond Flour and Pure Almond Extract

The pumpkin and pumpkin-friendly spices (cloves, cinnamon, allspice) in this cake meld surprisingly well with the chocolate chips studded throughout. This cake is an old favorite of our readers, with over 300 five-star reviews. Shop the recipe: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

We did the testing: This is the best way to keep your cheesecake from cracking.

Top with maple- or bourbon-spiked whipped cream to dress it up for the holiday; details are in the recipe tips at the bottom of our Homemade Whipped Cream recipe.

The texture of the filling is ultra-smooth and creamy, and the maple flavor is apparent, yet subtle — the secret is natural maple flavor paired with maple syrup. The pecan crust, meanwhile, is a nutty, salty counterbalance to the filling.

If you’re looking for a celebratory yet unexpected dessert for your table, we recommend this recipe. A heavy pour of Irish whiskey cream liqueur (save some for your after-dinner coffee!) flavors the smooth, light filling, while silky chocolate ganache adorns the top. Oven space at a premium while you prep Thanksgiving dinner? This dessert is no-bake, so you can save some room in the cooking schedule.

This flourless cake is incredibly rich — like sliceable fudge sauce. #9750. How Crypto Wallets Are Becoming More Than Just Wallets

At the beginning of Bitcoin, there was no such thing as a crypto wallet as we know it today. You had a full node, took care of complex private keys, and that was it. A lot has changed since then. Simpler and lighter apps appeared over the years, making it easier for users to manage their coins. But the evolution didn’t end there: now, crypto wallets are more than just wallets.

These versatile apps can do a lot of things beyond just storing funds, signing transactions, and sending payments. Of course, it always depends on the brand and network(s) involved, but we can find many interesting features to take advantage of in numerous crypto wallets. Let’s explore some of them.

Historically, people's "identity"—even in the digital realm—has always been assigned and managed by third parties (governments, corporations, etc.). However, the decentralized world offers an alternative through the self-sovereign identity (SSI) model. As the name implies, this is a form of identity or personal verification that can only be managed by the user who owns that identity.

In this way, very specific data can be shared only when necessary, rather than all personal information—for example, only age is verified, and the name is never revealed. Some crypto wallets can handle this type of digital ID already, in different ways. In an SSI setup, the wallet generally stores the credential and its cryptographic keys on the user's device. The issuer creates and signs the credential, while a decentralized network may store a DID (decentralized identifier), public key, credential schema, or revocation/status information that helps verify it.

When the user presents the credential, the recipient checks the issuer's signature and relevant on-chain data without needing the credential itself to be public. Examples of wallets that already have this feature include Dock Wallet, cheqd Wallet, Privado ID Wallet, and the Obyte Wallet. In the latter, you can verify your real name, your email, your GitHub account, your status as an accredited investor by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and more.

All of this is done via chatbots integrated into the same wallet. Then, the information is stored in your wallet, and you can selectively share parts of that information with whoever you like.

You can't communicate directly with your transaction peers in every crypto wallet, but you can in some of them—and with end-to-end encryption, too. You can even send messages on-chain, if you want, and enjoy some easier chatbots here and there. Depending on the system, messages may travel through a peer-to-peer network and be read only by the intended recipient, and never by someone else.

As for more public on-chain messages that will last forever, this can be done even on Bitcoin, but it’s not exactly user-friendly there. The process often involves converting your message to hexadecimal code, finding specific wallets that support this function or advanced features inside wallets, and pasting that hex code into a designated field, sending a transaction without funds. In other crypto networks and wallets, it’s just a matter of writing whatever you want in a user-friendly menu, pressing “send,” and paying a small transaction fee.

Chatbots aren’t that common, but they can be welcome, especially for beginners. They can respond to commands or help users perform actions from a familiar chat interface. They can be related to Large-Language Models (LLMs) like Plug Wallet or KaleidoSwap, or simply follow ingrained instructions without the risks associated with AI, like the Obyte Wallet. In the latter one, you can enjoy all of these features: encrypted chat, user-friendly on-chain messages, and classic chatbots.

These days, it’s rare that your crypto wallet can’t interact with smart contracts and make programmable transactions. Smart contracts are small computer programs stored in a certain ledger and designed to carry out specific, pre-set rules. They can automate payments, exchanges, loans, bets, games, and many other applications.

In practice, when you’re inside a crypto wallet, the most you will typically see regarding a smart contract is the permission requested by a specific Dapp to connect to your address and, likely, use some of your funds. Unless you are a developer, you probably have little idea how to "read" one—let alone create one. Most wallets won’t show you this, either, but there are some of them with friendlier smart contracts.

Obyte is one of them. You can create conditional payments and smart contracts in human language inside the app, all of it without coding and via encrypted chat.

Besides, if you’re sending a transaction or interacting with a Dapp, you’ll be able to see a clear preview of the results and fees before pressing “Send” or “Pay.”

Remember the familiar routine of creating a new account for every website? Wallet-based authentication offers another route. With Sign-In with Ethereum (SIWE), for instance, a user can prove control of an account by signing a message. The signature happens inside the wallet, while the application verifies it. The standard was designed to give Ethereum accounts a consistent way to authenticate with services outside the network itself.

This can make one on-chain account useful across multiple applications. The address acts as a persistent identity that can be used across many Dapps, with the wallet handling the signature needed to prove control. Beyond MetaMask for Ethereum, other providers of this feature include Para and WalletConnect for multiple networks.

Beyond your own businesses, you can also contribute to your community and help shape the future of your favorite networks by participating in governance. On-chain governance lets token holders vote on proposals whose results can trigger changes to a network’s rules, parameters, treasury, or other functions. The voting process and its powers vary from one network to another, but the wallet can provide the place where users review proposals, connect their address, and cast a vote with their governance tokens.

The mechanics can be quite simple. A proposal appears in a governance interface, the wallet shows the vote and any required transaction, and the user confirms it by signing. Some systems use delegated voting, so users can assign their voting power to another address instead. In other cases, holding a specific token or meeting a balance requirement determines who can participate.

Examples include MetaMask supporting governance voting through compatible Dapps, Keplr providing governance features for Cosmos networks, and Obyte allowing users to participate in on-chain voting through its wallet and governance website.

In the end, the word “wallet” is starting to sound a little undersized for all of this. The same account can connect a person to applications, support communication, authenticate access, interact with programmable software, and even decide on the future of a network. A crypto wallet remains a place to manage digital assets, but its role can extend much further, and it'll likely continue to do so.

#9749. My Worker Exited 0 With Jobs Still Marked "Running", and Nothing Retried Them

A deploy finished at 02:10, the supervisor logged a clean stop, and the worker exited with code 0. By 02:12 the queue depth graph was flat at zero, which looked like success and was actually the opposite. Work had been claimed, never finished, and the rows sat in running where no retry could see them. So what exactly happens to a job that is mid-flight when the platform sends SIGTERM?

My worker loop claims one row at a time from a jobs table, calls one outbound HTTP endpoint, then marks the row done. Each call has a 20-second client timeout, and the orchestrator allows 10 seconds between SIGTERM and SIGKILL. That mismatch alone guarantees the drain can never finish, but three smaller decisions turned it into a silent data problem instead of a loud crash.

Put those together and the failing path is boring: signal arrives, handler flips a flag, the main thread is still blocked inside a 20-second socket read, SIGKILL lands, and the row keeps status='running' for half an hour. Is your shutdown path covered by any test at all, or only by the deploy that happens to be quiet?

The useful part of this bug is that it is cheap to reproduce, because you only need real signals and a real process table. Save the worker as worker.py, then drive it from this script:

And inspect.py is deliberately dumb, because you want it to fail loudly:

Run it against the naive worker and you should see exactly the number of jobs that were in flight when the kill landed. Run it against a fixed worker and the count should be zero, or the rows should already be back in queued before your script checks. Label: the SQL below is reconstructed pseudo-Postgres, not a copy of production code; adapt the claim statement to your own store.

The first temptation is to "handle the signal properly", which does not help when the kill arrives mid-socket. The version that survived my next deploy had three parts.

The reaper then becomes a one-liner you can reason about, and its window is bounded by the heartbeat interval rather than by a 30-minute guess:

Keep the lease comfortably larger than the heartbeat plus the slowest single call, and check the numbers instead of vibes. One caveat that bit me: do not reuse the main connection inside the heartbeat thread, because most drivers are not thread-safe and you will get a confusing protocol error that looks like a database bug.

The shutdown deadline, the per-job timeout, and the platform grace period are three numbers that must agree, and I now write them in one table before touching the code.

If the platform grace is shorter than your worst-case drain, stop pretending you can drain: shorten the per-job timeout, cut concurrency to one at a time, and let the lease do the recovery work. Which of those three numbers did you actually measure, and which one did you copy from a sample config file?

Two parts of this loop are annoying to set up on a laptop, so I used MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option for them. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The free model was decent at the tedious part, turning a few thousand lines of claim/release log lines into an ordered timeline of stop_requested, last heartbeat, and kill, which is exactly the reading I am worst at doing patiently. The free server gave me a plain Linux shell where kill -TERM hits a real process and wait returns a real exit code, which is the whole point of the harness above.

What it did not do is decide the deadline numbers or tell me the reaper window was wrong, because a model reading logs only sees what I logged. The honest limitation is that if your worker never emits in_flight, no amount of summarising will recover it, so fix the log line first and paste it second.

The changes I would keep tomorrow are the harness (it runs in CI as a smoke test), the lease column with a heartbeat, and the event=stopped_with_work line that a grep can find during a post-deploy check. The sprint I would not repeat is the hour I spent adding a longer SIGTERM handler, which cannot help a thread that is blocked in a socket read.

Skip this approach if you are on a runtime with no signal semantics, if your grace period is under a second, or if you cannot add a lease column and a reaper. Also skip it if you need exactly-once processing, because a lease gives you at-least-once and your handler still has to be idempotent. If you want to rerun the harness without provisioning your own box, the free server option is a reasonable place to start, and the code above is the part worth copying.

#9745. Your Free Tier Is Not a Capacity Plan: Five Throughput Myths and a Concurrency Ramp

A demo handles one request at a time. A launch sends ten at once. The endpoint falls over.

Was the model worse today? Or did nobody measure the shape of the curve?

I keep seeing the same five claims about free models and free servers. Each one sounds reasonable. Each one falls apart under a ten-minute test.

I run these probes against MonkeyCode's free model access and its free server option while prototyping.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Nothing below depends on that relationship. Swap in any endpoint you control. The method is the point.

If one call takes two seconds, ten calls take twenty. Right?

No. That is a queue, not a multiplier. Little's Law says concurrency equals arrival rate multiplied by time in system. When arrivals outrun service capacity, waiting time stops being bounded.

The curve has a knee. Left of it, latency is flat. Right of it, latency goes vertical and errors appear.

You cannot read the knee in a doc page. You find it by ramping.

Retries feel like resilience. Under saturation they are a load multiplier.

Say a third of calls fail and you retry twice. Offered load can nearly double. At the knee, that turns a brownout into an outage.

A corrected model: retry only classified transient failures. Use exponential backoff with jitter. Keep a retry budget, something like ten percent of successful calls.

Primary sources worth reading: AWS on backoff and jitter and the SRE book chapter on handling overload.

Free tiers make people skip measurement. "It is just a prototype."

But the shape transfers. The knee moves. The existence of a knee does not.

A prototype that dies at ten users teaches you nothing. A prototype with a written envelope teaches you where the queue belongs.

A 429 is admission control talking. It says your offered load exceeded what the server will accept.

A timeout says your deadline was shorter than time to first byte.

Neither one is a bug report. Both are signals to slow down, queue, or shed.

Make 429 a first-class state in the client. Do not swallow it as an exception.

Without all five numbers, "the model is slow" is a guess with good manners.

Here is the probe. It is a template, not a run. I am not publishing numbers from it.

Stop rule first. Stop a level when either condition fires:

If rps flattens while p95 climbs, you are past the knee. More concurrency is now just more waiting.

Half the knee, not the knee. Headroom is for the day your prompt gets longer.

Now encode what you measured. Do not leave it in a notebook.

Retryable is yours to define. Map 429, 503, and connect timeouts to it. Map everything else to a hard failure.

So why ship a cap you never measured? You cannot defend a number you never took.

Run one ramp. Write the knee in your README. If you are prototyping on a budget, run the same script against MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option before you commit to a paid plan. The script does not care whose endpoint answers.

#9744. Small Tweaks, Great Output: What Merchants Can Do to Maximize Pay By Bank Conversion

Noda is an Open Banking technology provider.

Noda is an Open Banking technology provider.

Noda is an Open Banking technology provider.

Open banking payments are a genuinely good deal for merchants. Lower transaction fees than cards, near-instant access to settled funds, no card chargeback headaches. But in many markets, it's still a relatively new checkout option, and even where the infrastructure is mature (think the UK, the Netherlands or Germany), plenty of shoppers still default to what they know – cards, PayPal or other methods. In Central and Eastern Europe, awareness is growing fast, but it's still an education curve.

So how do you nudge your users to pick it? There are two ways to get there.

Some solutions, like Noda’s BIN-to-Bank, use smart routing through the card form to bring Pay by Bank into the payment flow without any changes to your checkout UI.

But if Pay by Bank is a visible option in your checkout, how it’s presented makes all the difference. We asked Lucy Oganisian, Product Designer at Noda, to share a few practical UX tweaks that can help merchants improve Pay by Bank conversion – whether you're running a WooCommerce store on a plugin that allows basic customisation or engineering a fully custom checkout from scratch.

Here's what actually works, tested and approved by our team.

Tests show that vague labels quietly kill conversion. Button names like "Bank transfer" or "Open Banking" leave users uncertain about what they're actually doing – and uncertain users don't convert.

“Pay by Bank” is becoming a recognizable standard in the same way "Pay by Card" is. Moreover, when "Pay by Card" and "Pay by Bank" sit next to each other, the choice feels obvious and balanced, not like one is the main event and the other is a footnote.

The same applies to localised checkouts: clear and direct translations tend to perform better than more creative alternatives.

When a payment method is unfamiliar, users look for anchors they already trust. Bank logos are one of the most powerful trust signals you can add, and they cost nothing to display.

A small row of recognisable bank marks near your Pay by Bank option signals two things: this is real, and my bank is probably here. That second part matters a lot. Users want to know their specific institution is supported before they proceed further.

Some providers like Trustly or Klarna push their own branding at this touchpoint, but that tells users very little if they've never heard of them. Familiar bank marks work like trust badges but more credible – because they're institutions users already rely on.

Hiding the Pay by Bank option below the fold is a pain point that hits hardest on mobile. If users need to scroll to discover it, it becomes the "backup plan" option, not a first choice. And that's exactly how it'll convert.

A couple of things to avoid: placing it out of the visible area on load, and creating multiple equally prominent buttons on one screen. When users face two "main" actions, they hesitate.

As for where exactly to put it: in markets where Pay by Bank is already a well-known checkout option, don't hesitate to place it first. In markets where awareness is still building, second position works nicely – visible and clearly labelled but not demanding attention before the user is ready.

Placing individual bank buttons directly into your checkout can be a great way to minimize further screens and potential drop-offs – especially for e-commerce flows.

But there's a ceiling. In many European markets, the top 3–5 banks cover roughly 70–90% of users, so a short preview serves the majority without cluttering the experience. Showing, for example, 5 banks tends to outperform showing 9: decisions feel easier, the flow stays pleasant, and conversion follows. The rest can live behind a "show more" option – accessible, but out of the way.

It’'s best to pick button colours that are consistent with your website. If the Pay by Bank button style clashes with your site's design – users notice, even if they can't articulate why.

The same goes for typography: text that fails to meet WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) requirements can easily become unreadable, often due to low contrast or font size. It excludes some users and signals a lack of polish to the rest.

If you're using a plugin and your provider offers customisation features, spend a few minutes on the appearance settings after setup. It's among the quickest, highest-return things you can do.

None of this requires significant technical investment. But these details do shape how Pay by Bank is perceived at checkout. Pay by Bank is often viewed as an attractive option for merchants. A few thoughtful tweaks can make it the more obvious choice for their customers too. What often determines uptake is how naturally the option appears in the user journey. When Pay by Bank feels visible, trustworthy and well-integrated, customers are far more likely to choose it.

#9739. Building a Charge Page Template for a Criminal Defense Site

If you build or maintain a website for a criminal defense firm, most of your work will end up in one template: the charge page. A typical defense site has twenty to sixty of them, one for each offense the firm handles, sometimes split by county or by first and repeat offenses. They bring in most of the search traffic and most of the calls.

A good charge page template makes those pages easy for lawyers and editors to write, consistent for readers and fast on a phone. A weak one turns every new page into a custom design job. This post covers how to design the template from the content model up, with notes from the kinds of problems that show up on real law firm sites.

Before opening a design tool, define the fields a charge page needs. Lawyers think in terms of the charge, the possible penalties, the court process and common defenses. The CMS should reflect that so editors fill in structured fields rather than one large rich text box.

The last_reviewed field matters more than it looks. Penalties and procedures change, and a visible review date helps both readers and the firm keep pages accurate.

Most people reach a charge page from a phone, often in a stressful moment. The first screen should show the charge name as the heading, a short opening that speaks to the reader's situation and a clear way to call. Large hero images push all of that below the fold, so keep them small or leave them out.

Each field in the content model should map to a section component with fixed styling. Editors choose the content, not the fonts, colors or spacing. That keeps forty charge pages looking like one site rather than forty experiments.

Navigation matters as the number of charge pages grows. This guide on building a menu for a defense firm with many practice areas covers how to group charges so visitors and crawlers can find them.

Charge pages compete in local search, and page experience is part of what Google considers. Watch the Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift. On law firm sites, the usual causes of trouble are oversized hero images, chat widgets that load early and block the main thread, and fonts or embeds that shift the layout as they load.

Set explicit dimensions on images and embeds. Load third-party chat and tracking scripts after the main content. Self-host fonts or limit the number of weights. Test on a mid-range Android phone over a throttled connection rather than only on a fast laptop.

Lawyers need to review penalty and process content before it goes live. Build a draft and review state into the CMS workflow, and record who approved each page. Attorney advertising rules vary by state, and some require disclaimers on certain pages. Add a disclaimer field or a site-wide component that can be switched on per page rather than hard-coding text.

Accessibility belongs in the template too. Use proper heading order, sufficient color contrast and form labels that screen readers can announce. A person in crisis may be using assistive technology, and an inaccessible contact form loses calls.

For more design ideas aimed at defense practices, see the collection of law firm website design guides.

No. A shared template with structured fields keeps the site consistent and makes maintenance far easier. Variation should come from the content.

Use the same template with a jurisdiction field and require unique local content, such as the courthouse and local process, so the pages are not near-duplicates.

Generate it from the structured fields so it stays in sync with the visible content. Only mark up what is actually on the page.

#9737. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9731. Make Grilled Cheese Macedonian-Style For Double The Cheese & Flavor

Although less-famed than neighboring Greek and not-too-distant Turkish cooking, Northern Macedonian cuisine contains an abundance of delicious offerings. A mix of Balkan, Slavic, Mediterranean, and Middle Eastern influences, there's a lot to take from this regional culinary style. You can even infuse a Macedonian flair into grilled cheese by making a dish called przeni lepcinja.

Reminiscent of French toast but with a distinctly Mediterranean flair, this meal makes for a savvy way to use stale bread. Thick slices of bread — typically sourdough — are soaked in an egg and milk mixture, then layered with a generous dose of shredded mozzarella in between. This sandwich is then pan-fried in aromatic olive oil, thereby forming a golden-brown, bready dish, stuffed with gooey cheese inside. Scattered with feta atop before serving, it's an international grilled cheese style worth trying.

After all, feta and eggs are a tried-and-true pairing; the cheese is salty and tangy and adds a complex dimension to breakfast food. Meanwhile, that interior mozz melts down into creamy-gooey goodness that's still quintessentially a grilled cheese. The dish comes together with pantry staples, but presents the elements in a creative new form.

The classic przeni lepcinja formula is delicious, but the dish welcomes other components, too. Cheese is an important part of Macedonian cuisine – as well as Balkan food broadly — so tracking down regional cheese varieties can give your przeni lepcinja an extra-flavorful flair. Look out for belo sirenje, a crumbly white cheese reminiscent of feta, but crafted according to Macedonian techniques. Often made with sheep's milk, you can substitute it with Greek Sheep Milk Feta, a product that's easier to find in the United States.

Don't rule out enhancing the Macedonian grilled cheese stuffing, either. Chop up some tomatoes and peppers for a touch of sweetness. Or add some ajvar, a relish made with roasted eggplants and bell peppers. The condiment is also popular in Macedonia, and oftentimes served alongside cheese. Finally, round out your przeni lepcinja with ham, which will add both salt and meatiness to the dish. If the components are difficult to fit alongside the mozzarella, scoop out some of the bread's interior — the egg binder will hold the sandwich together. Flavorful and easy-to-make, przeni lepcinja is worth including in the weeknight rotation.
